one_liner: Concurrent in-memory trie of B+-trees with ordered range scans; authors measured 1.5-3.7x Redis 2.4 throughput on 16 cores.
what_it_does: Masstree is a research key-value store from MIT and Harvard: one ordered in-memory index shared by all cores, plus an optional server (mtd) with per-core logging and periodic checkpoints for persistence. It supports get, put, remove and ordered range scans (getrange) on binary keys of up to 255 bytes by default, with values split into numbered columns. It is not Redis-compatible: the server speaks its own msgpack protocol over TCP/UDP (Get/Scan/Put/Replace/Remove/Checkpoint). Embedding the tree means using C++ templates (basic_table, tcursor, scan) with a threadinfo object per thread.
how_it_is_fast: Keys are cut into 8-byte slices stored as byte-swapped 64-bit integers, so each trie layer is a fanout-15 B+-tree that compares keys with plain integer compares (the paper credits this with 13-19%) and compares a long shared prefix only once per layer. Nodes are four cache lines and are prefetched whole before use, so each level costs about one DRAM latency. Readers use optimistic concurrency control (they check per-node version counters, take no locks and never write shared memory), while writers lock only the nodes they touch, publish a leaf insert in one step through a 64-bit permutation field, and free nodes through epoch-based (RCU-like) reclamation. The paper's factor analysis also credits a fast allocator and 2 MB superpages with a 27-37% gain.
when_to_use: You need an ordered in-memory index with range scans that many threads share, for example the index layer of an in-memory database or transactional store where a hash table cannot serve scans.

Access is skewed (Zipfian) on a multicore box. At the paper's highest skew (delta=9), one shared Masstree delivered 3.5x the throughput of 16 hard-partitioned instances, which stall on the hot partition.
Keys share long prefixes (URLs, hierarchical or composite keys). The trie layers compare each 8-byte slice once instead of re-comparing the whole key at every tree level.
Workloads are small-key, small-value and read-heavy on x86-64 Linux. The paper measured 9-10M gets/s on 16 cores with networking and logging included.
You want a reference design or research baseline. HN commenters note Masstree became a standard comparator in key-value store papers.
when_not_to_use: You want a Redis replacement. It has no RESP protocol, rich data types, TTLs or eviction (none found in the source), replication or clustering, and mtd is a research-grade server.

You only do point lookups on uniform keys. The paper's own concurrent hash table reached 2.5x Masstree's throughput, 16 hard-partitioned Masstrees beat the shared tree by 1.5x on uniform gets, and memcached 1.4.8 was 7.4% faster on uniform gets.

You target anything other than x86. The master branch hard-codes x86 inline asm (pause, mfence, prefetcht0, bswapq, rdtsc), and its acquire/release fences are compiler-only barriers that rely on x86 ordering. The arm64 port (PR #31) has been open and unmerged since 2018.

You need an actively maintained dependency. The last commit was 2023-10-12, it has one old tag (v0.9.0) and no GitHub releases, and 9 issues remain open, including a scan race (#33) and empty leftmost leaves that are not freed after deleting all keys (#43).
Your legal review cannot approve a custom license. It is MIT plus W3C-style publicity and title clauses, and GitHub shows NOASSERTION.

integration.dependencies: pthreads and libm. autoconf (2.69) is needed to bootstrap the build. Optional: jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc, Hoard or Flow as the malloc, and libnuma.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 language features are required. configure retries with -std=gnu++1y and its error message asks for C++14. It needs GCC or Clang with GNU inline asm and __sync builtins. C++20/23 warnings were fixed in 2023 (PR #48).
integration.platforms: x86-64 only on master. The README says it is tested on Debian, Ubuntu and macOS, and a FreeBSD build fix was merged (PR #32).
integration.thread_safety: Built for concurrency: many threads can get, put, remove and scan one table, each with its own threadinfo. Gets are lock-free optimistic reads and writers take per-node spinlocks. Scans are not atomic with respect to concurrent inserts or updates. Memory is reclaimed only if the embedder advances the global epoch and calls rcu_quiesce.

gotchas: Embedding it means defining the globals the library expects (globalepoch, active_epoch and recovering, as unit-mt.cc does), creating a threadinfo per thread, and advancing epochs or calling rcu_quiesce regularly. Without that, freed nodes accumulate in per-thread limbo lists.

Key handling does intentional 'sloppy' reads that can touch up to 8 bytes outside the key buffer (the preconditions are documented in string_slice.hh). Open issue #42 reports a possible segfault for key lengths that are not a multiple of 8, so pad key buffers and expect sanitizer reports.

The write API is low-level. tcursor.find_insert() or find_locked() locks the leaf, you write lp.value(), and lp.finish(+1/0/-1, ti) must always be called because it applies the insert or remove and releases the lock.

Assertions are compiled in by default. The README says to build with ./configure --disable-assertions before measuring performance, and the tree's node allocations go through the threadinfo pool allocator, so the malloc you link affects results.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Masstree over MICA or MemC3 when you need ordered keys and range scans: both are hash-based, and MICA's paper reports 75.5-76.9 Mops against Masstree's 16.5 on tiny point operations. Prefer it over Garnet, Dragonfly or Valkey only if you are building your own storage engine and want an embeddable concurrent ordered index rather than a maintained server that speaks the Redis protocol.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' EuroSys 2012 paper, on 16 cores of a 2.4 GHz AMD Opteron 8431 server with networking and logging on, the full Masstree server did 9.10M uniform gets/s against 5.97M for 16 Redis 2.4.5 processes, 5.84M puts/s against 2.97M, and 6.05-9.86M against 2.13-2.70M on Zipfian MYCSB-A/B/C (about 1.5-3.7x), while memcached 1.4.8 was 7.4% faster on uniform gets. No compiler or flags are given, the baselines date from 2011, and the paper itself calls the comparisons 'not entirely fair'.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2023-10-12, no GitHub releases, arm64 PR never merged) and under a custom MIT-plus-W3C-clause license, so treat it as a reference design to study, or to vendor after legal review, rather than a maintained dependency.
